claims.statement: The bakunawa, the Philippine moon-eating dragon, is a dragon-like serpent of Philippine mythology causing natural phenomena, mainly eclipses; its movements were a geomantic calendar and part of babaylan rituals; it has a looped tail and one nose horn and lives in the sky or underworld.
claims.statement_id: Bakunawa, naga pemakan bulan dari Filipina, adalah ular mirip naga dalam mitologi Filipina yang menyebabkan gejala alam, terutama gerhana; gerakannya menjadi penanggalan geomantik dan bagian ritual babaylan; berekor melingkar dan bertanduk satu di hidung; tinggal di langit atau dunia bawah.
claims.quote: is a dragon-like serpent in Philippine mythology that causes several natural phenomena, primarily eclipses. The movements of the Bakunawa served as a geomantic calendar system for ancient Filipinos and were part of the rituals of the babaylan priestess. It is usually depicted with a characteristic looped tail and a single horn on the nose.

claims.statement: Through trade with South Asia and Indianization, the bakunawa was syncretized with the Nāga, Rahu and Ketu of Hindu-Buddhist mythology.
claims.statement_id: Karena hubungan dagang dengan Asia Selatan dan indianisasi Asia Tenggara, bakunawa dilebur dengan Naga, Rahu, dan Ketu dari mitologi Hindu-Buddha.
claims.quote: Due to increasing trade contacts with South Asia and the Indianization of Southeast Asia, the Bakunawa later became syncretized with the Nāga, Rahu, and Ketu of Hindu-Buddhist mythology.

claims.statement: Bakunawa is thought to be a compound meaning 'bent snake', from Proto-Western-Malayo-Polynesian *ba(ŋ)kuq ('bent') and *sawa ('large snake'); variants include Vakonawa, Baconaua, Bakonaua.
claims.statement_id: Bakunawa diduga kata majemuk berarti 'ular bengkok', dari Proto-Melayu-Polinesia Barat *ba(ŋ)kuq ('bengkok') dan *sawa ('ular besar'); ejaan lain Vakonawa, Baconaua, Bakonaua.
claims.quote: Bakunawa is believed to be originally a compound word meaning "bent snake", from Proto-Western-Malayo-Polynesian *ba(ŋ)kuq ("bent", "curved") and *sawa ("large snake", "python"). Spelling variants include Vakonawa, Baconaua, or Bakonaua.

claims.statement: The most similar is the Tagalog Laho (from Rahu), a serpent-like dragon causing lunar eclipses.
claims.statement_id: Yang paling mirip bakunawa adalah Laho dari Tagalog (dari Rahu), naga mirip ular penyebab gerhana bulan.
claims.quote: The most similar to the Bakunawa is the Tagalog Laho (derived from Rahu; also known as Nono or Buaya), a serpent-like dragon that causes moon eclipses.

claims.statement: Pre-colonial Cebuanos believed the supreme god Bathala made 7 moons; the bakunawa, amazed, rose from the sea and swallowed them, becoming Bathala's mortal enemy.
claims.statement_id: Orang Cebuano prakolonial percaya dewa tertinggi Bathala menciptakan 7 bulan; bakunawa yang terpesona bangkit dari laut dan menelannya, sehingga menjadi musuh Bathala.
claims.quote: pre-colonial Cebuanos believed that their supreme god—Bathala, or Kaptan the Visayan tradition—created 7 moons to illuminate the night sky. The Bakunawa, amazed by their beauty, would rise from the ocean and swallow the moons whole, angering Bathala and causing them to be mortal enemies.

claims.statement: To stop the moons being devoured, early Filipinos clanged pots and pans outdoors to startle the bakunawa into disgorging them.
claims.statement_id: Agar bulan tidak habis ditelan, orang Filipina dahulu keluar rumah memukul panci dan wajan agar bakunawa terkejut dan memuntahkan bulan.
claims.quote: To prevent the complete devouring of the moons, early Filipinos would rush outdoors, clanging pots and pans to startle the Bakunawa into disgorging the moons.

claims.statement: According to Jordan Clark, most recent literary versions derive from Damiana Eugenio's retelling, itself imagined from Fernando Buyser's earlier account.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Jordan Clark, tafsiran sastra terkini tentang bakunawa bersumber dari penceritaan ulang Damiana Eugenio, yang dibayangkan dari catatan Fernando Buyser sebelumnya.
claims.quote: Most of the recent literary interpretations of Bakunawa can be sourced to renowned folklorist Damiana Eugenio’s re-telling of the myth in her collected compilation “Philippine Folk Literature: The Myths“. This, however, was imagined from an earlier documentation by Fernando Buyser

claims.statement: The first documentation of the bakunawa was in 1628 by Fr. Alonso de Mentrida, an Augustinian missionary, in a Hiligaynon dictionary.
claims.statement_id: Dokumentasi pertama tentang bakunawa dibuat pada 1628 oleh Fr. Alonso de Mentrida, misionaris Agustinian, dalam kamus bahasa Hiligaynon.
claims.quote: the first documentation about Bakunawa in 1628 by Fr. Alonso de Mentrida, who was an Augustinian missionary

claims.statement: The bakunawa was believed to live in the sky or the underworld.
claims.statement_id: Bakunawa diyakini tinggal di langit atau di dunia bawah.
claims.quote: It was believed to inhabit either the sky or the underworld.

claims.statement: Phra Siam Devadhiraj (พระสยามเทวาธิราช) is a guardian deity personifying supernatural protection over Thailand; the deva (sometimes 'god' or 'angel') is represented by an idol in the Phaisan Thaksin Throne Hall of the Grand Palace.
claims.statement_id: Phra Siam Devadhiraj (พระสยามเทวาธิราช) adalah dewa pelindung yang mempersonifikasikan perlindungan gaib atas Thailand; dewa ini (deva, kata asal Sanskerta yang kadang diterjemahkan 'dewa' atau 'malaikat') diwujudkan dalam arca di Balairung Phaisan Thaksin, Istana Agung.
claims.quote: Phra Siam Devadhiraj (Thai: พระสยามเทวาธิราช, RTGS: Phra Sayam Thewathirat) is a guardian deity personifying supernatural protection over the country of Thailand. The deity (deva, a sanskrit origin word, sometimes translated as "god" or "angel") is represented by an idol enshrined in the Phaisan Thaksin Throne Hall of the Grand Palace.

claims.statement: The 8-inch (200 mm) solid gold statue was commissioned by King Mongkut (Rama IV), probably around 1859–1860, showing the deva in royal dress with a sword and a blessing gesture.
claims.statement_id: Arca emas murni setinggi 8 inci (200 mm) itu dibuat atas perintah Raja Mongkut (Rama IV), kemungkinan sekitar 1859–1860, dan menggambarkan sang dewa berbusana raja, memegang pedang, dengan sikap tangan memberkati.
claims.quote: The statue, 8 in (200 mm) tall and made of solid gold, was commissioned by King Mongkut (Rama IV), probably around the years 1859–1860. It shows the deva in royal dress, holding a sword in the right hand and with the left hand at chest level in a blessing posture.

claims.statement: The deity is worshipped in an annual private royal ceremony on the first waxing moon of the fifth Thai lunar month, the traditional New Year.
claims.statement_id: Dewa ini dipuja dalam upacara kerajaan tertutup setiap tahun pada hari pertama bulan naik di bulan kelima penanggalan Thai, Tahun Baru tradisional.
claims.quote: The deity is worshipped in an annual private royal ceremony on the first waxing moon of the fifth Thai lunar month, which marks the traditional New Year in the Thai lunar calendar.

claims.statement: In Philippine mythology, the siyokoy (also shokoy, syokoy, siokoy) is an aquatic humanoid with scales, webbed limbs and fins; most legends make it hostile, drowning people.
claims.statement_id: Dalam mitologi Filipina, siyokoy (juga shokoy, syokoy, siokoy) adalah makhluk air mirip manusia bersisik, bertungkai berselaput, dan bersirip; kebanyakan legenda menyebutnya memusuhi manusia dan menenggelamkan orang.
claims.quote: In Philippine mythology, a siyokoy (also shokoy, syokoy or siokoy) is an aquatic humanoid creature often described as having scales, webbed limbs, and fins. Most legends characterise siyokoy as hostile to humans, and they are said to drown individuals.

claims.statement: Siyokoy comes from Hokkien shui gui ('water ghost'); in Chinese folklore shui gui are drowned spirits who drag victims underwater to possess their bodies.
claims.statement_id: Istilah siyokoy berasal dari Hokkien shui gui ('hantu air'); dalam cerita rakyat Tionghoa, shui gui adalah arwah orang tenggelam yang menyeret korban ke air untuk merasuki tubuhnya.
claims.quote: The term siyokoy came from the Hokkien shui gui. In Chinese folklore, shui gui are the restless spirits of drowned people, who drag unsuspecting victims underwater and drown them in order to possess their bodies.

claims.statement: In modern Tagalog folklore, siyokoy are sea monsters, humanlike with glistening brown or green scales and webbed feet, who drown fishermen and eat them.
claims.statement_id: Dalam cerita rakyat Tagalog modern, siyokoy adalah monster laut mirip manusia bersisik ikan cokelat atau hijau berkilau dan berkaki berselaput, yang menenggelamkan nelayan lalu memakannya.
claims.quote: In modern Tagalog folklore, siyokoy are sea monsters, an anthropoid whose body is covered in glistening brown or green fish scales and webbet feet

claims.statement: Siyokoy drown fishermen and eat them.
claims.statement_id: Siyokoy menenggelamkan nelayan dan memakannya.
claims.quote: they drown fishermen and consume them for food.

claims.statement: Engkanto (from Spanish encanto, 'enchantment') are environmental spirits able to appear in human form, often linked with ancestral spirits and spirits of the dead called anito in the Philippines.
claims.statement_id: Engkanto (dari bahasa Spanyol encanto, 'pesona') adalah roh lingkungan yang dapat menampakkan diri dalam wujud manusia, sering dikaitkan dengan arwah leluhur dan roh orang mati yang disebut anito di Filipina.
claims.quote: are mythical environmental spirits that are said to have the ability to appear in human form. They are often associated with the spirits of ancestors and spirits of the dead called anito in the Philippines.

claims.statement: The term was adopted from the Spanish, who, bewildered by the many mythical races in the Philippines, called many of them 'enchanted'.
claims.statement_id: Istilah ini diambil dari orang Spanyol yang bingung menghadapi beragamnya makhluk mitos di Filipina dan menyebut banyak di antaranya 'terpesona'.
claims.quote: The term itself was adopted from the Spanish, who were dumbfounded by the wide array of mythical races in the Philippines and just referred to many of the races as "enchanted".

claims.statement: Engkanto resemble humans: they age, have male and female sexes, can fall ill and even die; some are beautiful with blue eyes, fair skin and golden hair.
claims.statement_id: Engkanto mirip manusia: mereka menua, berjenis kelamin laki-laki dan perempuan, dapat sakit, bahkan mati; sebagian rupawan bermata biru, berkulit terang, dan berambut keemasan.
claims.quote: Engkanto have many similarities to humans in that they age, appear to have male and female sexes, can experience from illness and even die.

claims.statement: Their dwellings usually look like large rocks, trees or shadows, but appear as magnificent palaces to befriended humans; they prefer large trees like the balete.
claims.statement_id: Tempat tinggal mereka biasanya tampak seperti batu besar, pohon, atau bayangan, tetapi tampak sebagai istana megah bagi manusia yang mereka jadikan teman; mereka menyukai pohon besar seperti balete.
claims.quote: Their dwellings will normally appear as natural features such as large rocks, trees, or shadows in human form, although they can appear as magnificent palaces to humans they have befriended. These creatures prefer large trees and natural features such as the balete

claims.statement: Those the engkanto disfavour become depressed, mad or vanish for days or months, possibly through possession; they cause fevers and skin disease; anting-anting or agimat amulets ward them off, and favoured people gain power and riches.
claims.statement_id: Orang yang tidak disukai engkanto menjadi murung, gila, atau menghilang berhari-hari hingga berbulan-bulan, mungkin karena dirasuki; engkanto juga dapat menyebabkan demam dan penyakit kulit; jimat anting-anting atau agimat menangkalnya, dan orang yang mereka sukai memperoleh kekuatan dan kekayaan.
claims.quote: Those who the engkanto do not favor would become depressed, suffer from madness, or even disappear for days or months, possibly as a result of possession. They are also said to be capable of causing fevers and skin diseases such as boils.

claims.statement: Francisco Demetrio studied 87 folk stories from the Visayas and Mindanao on engkanto and argued they were based on early European friars.
claims.statement_id: Francisco Demetrio meneliti 87 cerita rakyat dari Visayas dan Mindanao tentang engkanto dan berpendapat engkanto didasarkan pada biarawan Eropa awal.
claims.quote: Francisco Demetrio made a study of 87 folk stories from Visayas and Mindanao relating to engkanto. He contended that the engkanto were based on early European friars.

claims.statement: According to Jordan Clark, the evolution of folklore creatures almost always begins with belief in these spirits.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Jordan Clark, evolusi makhluk folklor hampir selalu berawal dari kepercayaan pada roh-roh ini.
claims.quote: The evolution of folkloric creatures almost always begins with the belief in these spirits.

claims.statement: The engkanto of Philippine mythology are highly similar to the elves of European folklore.
claims.statement_id: Engkanto dalam mitologi Filipina sangat mirip dengan peri (elf) dalam cerita rakyat Eropa.
claims.quote: The engkanto of Philippine mythology are highly similar to elves of European folklore.

claims.statement: The Manaul (also Manaol) is a Philippine folklore bird with at least four stories; the name is also the common name of two large Philippine eagles, the Philippine eagle and white-bellied sea eagle.
claims.statement_id: Burung Manaul (juga Manaol) adalah makhluk cerita rakyat Filipina dengan sedikitnya empat kisah; nama ini juga nama umum dua elang besar Filipina, elang Filipina dan elang laut perut putih.
claims.quote: The Manaul bird is a creature of Philippine folklore. There are at least four existing stories regarding Manaul. "Manaul" (also spelled "Manaol") is also the native common name of two species of large eagles in the Philippines, the Philippine eagle and the white-bellied sea eagle.

claims.statement: A Manaul bird is mentioned in the Code of Kalantiaw from Panay, which makes killing it punishable by death.
claims.statement_id: Burung Manaul disebut dalam Kode Kalantiaw dari Pulau Panay, yang menyatakan membunuh burung ini dihukum mati.
claims.quote: A Manaul bird was mentioned in the Code of Kalantiaw, a sacred code from the island of Panay. According to this document, the killing of this bird is punishable by death.

claims.statement: In Mangyan and Negrito folklore, Manaul was a wrathful king imprisoned by King Tubluck Lawi; escaping, he rebelled against the gods, and the rocks Kaptan threw at him missed and became islands.
claims.statement_id: Dalam cerita rakyat Mangyan dan Negrito, Manaul adalah raja pemarah yang dipenjarakan Raja Tubluck Lawi; setelah lolos ia memberontak kepada semua dewa, dan batu-batu yang dilemparkan Kaptan kepadanya meleset dan menjadi pulau.
claims.quote: In Mangyan and Negrito folklore, Manaul was a wrathful king who was imprisoned by King Tubluck Lawi. When Manaul escaped, he later rebelled against all gods and spirits and was punished by Kaptan by throwing rocks at him. The rocks missed Manaul, and created islands

claims.statement: In Tagalog folklore, Bathala sent a tigmamanukan omen bird named Manaul to peck the bamboo; it split open, releasing the first man, Malakas, and the first woman, Maganda; Manaul then flew right to left as a good omen; other sources say Amihan in bird form pecked it.
claims.statement_id: Dalam cerita rakyat Tagalog, Bathala mengutus burung pertanda tigmamanukan bernama Manaul untuk mematuk bambu; bambu terbelah dan keluarlah laki-laki pertama, Malakas, dan perempuan pertama, Maganda; Manaul lalu terbang dari kanan ke kiri sebagai pertanda baik; sumber lain menyebut Amihan dalam wujud burung yang mematuknya.
claims.quote: In Tagalog folklore, it is said that Bathala sent a tigmamanukan omen bird he named "Manaul" to peck on the bamboo. Manaul flew from one side to the other before settling on the bamboo. When Manaul pecked on the bamboo, it opened in half and released the first man, Malakas, and the first woman, Maganda.

claims.statement: Historians now generally accept that the Code of Kalantiaw documents appear to be deliberate fabrications, written in 1913 by Jose Marco.
claims.statement_id: Para sejarawan kini umumnya menerima bahwa dokumen Kode Kalantiaw tampaknya rekaan yang disengaja tanpa nilai sejarah, ditulis pada 1913 oleh Jose Marco.
claims.quote: It is now generally accepted by historians that the documents supporting the existence and history of the code, according to some sources, "appear to be deliberate fabrications with no historical validity" written in 1913 by a scholar named Jose Marco

claims.statement: According to Jordan Clark, the Pavón manuscripts' trail leads to the 20th-century forger José E. Marco; the Manaul story is worth reading as folklore history, but the manuscript cannot authenticate it as ancient Visayan.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Jordan Clark, jejak dokumen naskah Pavón mengarah ke pemalsu barang antik abad ke-20 José E. Marco; kisah Manaul layak dibaca sebagai bagian sejarah folklor Filipina, tetapi naskah itu tidak dapat membuktikannya sebagai kisah Visayas kuno.
claims.quote: Its documentary trail leads instead to the twentieth-century antiquarian and forger José E. Marco. Manaul’s story remains worth reading as part of the history of Philippine folklore, but the manuscript cannot authenticate it as an ancient Visayan account.

claims.statement: The fullest named Manaul account comes through the so-called Pavón manuscripts.
claims.statement_id: Kisah Manaul yang paling lengkap berasal dari apa yang disebut naskah Pavón.
claims.quote: The fullest named account comes through the so-called Pavón manuscripts.
